message.content:
The answer is no for genuine finite expectations.
If X is a discrete random variable, its expectation is finite only when the positive and negative parts are both finite.
That condition is the same as saying that the expected absolute value of X is finite.
The same condition holds for Y if its expectation is finite.
For any two random variables, the triangle inequality holds pointwise.
Specifically, the absolute value of X plus Y is at most the sum of the absolute values.
Taking expectations preserves this inequality.
Therefore the expected absolute value of X plus Y is at most the sum of the expected absolute values.
Since both expected absolute values are finite, their sum is finite.
Hence X plus Y has finite expected absolute value.
That means the expectation of X plus Y is well defined.
It cannot be undefined or infinite.
The reason is that finite expectation already rules out conditional convergence trouble.
A discrete sum may look conditionally convergent, but expectation uses positive and negative parts.
Those parts must converge separately for a finite expectation.
When both variables have separately convergent positive and negative parts, the sum remains integrable.
This is a standard consequence of the linearity of expectation for integrable random variables.
One can also see it through the definition of discrete sums.
The probabilities form a countable mass function, and the values are multiplied by probabilities.
If both series for the positive and negative parts are finite, the combined series is controlled.
No cancellation can create an undefined or infinite expectation for the sum.
Thus the proposed scenario does not exist under the usual definition of finite expectation.
In conclusion, if the discrete random variables X and Y each have finite expectation, their sum also has finite expectation, so the requested construction is impossible under the usual definitions of probability theory beneath the standard rules.
